ĕquĕs, ĭtis, m.
id.
,
a horseman, rider.
In gen.: it eques et plausu cava concutit ungula terram, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 419 ed. Vahlen); ; ; ; (of Castor; cf. ; ); (of Bellerophon; cf. ); ; —Poet. transf.,

of horse and rider: quadrupes, Enn. ap. ; ; and (who, like the other ancient grammarians, consider eques = equus); cf. Enn. ed. Vahl. p. 37; imitated by Heyne.— Far more frequently,

In partic.
In milit. lang., a horse-soldier, trooper; opp. pedes, a foot-soldier, (twice); 1, 18 fin.; 1, 23, 2 et saep.; opp. pedites,; 2, 24, 1; 4, 33, 3 et saep.; opp. viri or homines, for pedites,; : equites singulares Augusti, v. singularis.—
Meton. or collect., horse-soldiers, cavalry: plurimum in Aetolis equitibus praesidii fuit: is longe tum optimus eques in Graecia erat,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Equites, the order of knights, the Equites, who, among the Romans, held a middle rank between the Senate and the Plebs, consisting, under Romulus, of the 300 Celeres, but whose number, as early as the reign of Tullus Hostilius, had increased to 18 centuries. In the last centuries of the republic this order enjoyed great consideration and influence in the conduct of public affairs, in consequence of the wealth they acquired as farmers of the public taxes, as also by reason of the right to the administration of justice held by them after the year 632 A. U. C. (acc. to the lex Sempronia judiciaria), ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. Dict. of Antiq., art. Equites. —
In the sing. collect., the equestrian order: senatores, eques, miles,; ; ; ; ; ; ;

senses: for my part, as far as I am concerned, as for me
la:adv:equidem.html:
ĕquĭdem, adv.
comp. of the interj. ĕ and quidem enclit.; cf. edepol
, a demonstrative corroborative particle,
verily, truly, indeed, at all events, = certe, revera, etc. (freq. and class.).
In gen.
Without other particles.
With 1. pers. in affirming a fact concerning one's self, or confirming a previous remark; equidem Sosia Amphitruonis sum,; ; : i in malam rem. Mi. Ibi sum equidem, : nihil inquit, equidem novi,: equidem et ante hoc tempus te dilexi,: equidem etiam illud mihi animum advertisse videor,; cf. Caes. ap. : id equidem ego certo scio,; so with ego,; , acc. to ; ; Kritz.; .—
With the 1. pers. plur.: equidem, ere, nos jam dudum hic te apsentem incusamus, ; so (but not in Cicero, Horace, Vergil, or Quintilian; v. Rib. Lat. Part. p. 37; Madv. ad ).—
With the 2. and 3. perss. sing. (perh. not in Plaut.; v. Ritschl, prol. ad Trin. p. 76 sq.; corrected, quidem, Stich. 2, 2, 5; 4, 1, 48; Mil. 3, 1, 55 Fleck.; Men. 2, 2, 35 Brix, etc. But quando equidem nec tibi bene esse pote pati, etc., Trin. 2, 2, 71 Ritschl2: atque equidem ipsus ultro venit, Ritschl2; cf. R): scitis equidem milites, etc.,; cf. ; : vanum equidem hoc consilium est,.—
With 3. pers. plur.: equidem innumerabiles mihi videntur,: per me equidem sint omnia alba,: equidem si nobis religiones nullae essent,: adulescentem equidem dicebant emisse, etc.,.—
Sometimes made more emphatic by certe, edepol, ecastor, hercle, etc. (most freq. in Plaut.): certe equidem noster sum,; so ; ; cf.: equidem certo idem sum,: credo edepol equidem dormire solem,: equidem pol,; ; : certe equidem edepol,; cf. with 3. pers.: equidem edepol liberali'st,: equidem ecastor vigilo,; : equidem hercle,; ; ; ; ; .—
In partic.
Certainly, by all means, of course, to be sure, in a concessive sense. Pi. Sine. Ba. Sino equidem, si lubet, ; . Q. Sed perge cetera. M. Pergam equidem, .— So with sed, verum, tamen, etc.: dixi equidem, sed, etc.,: sic ego nolim equidem apud rusticos, sed multo minus apud vos,; cf. : quibus epistolis sum equidem abs te lacessitus ad scribendum, sed, etc.,; cf. with foll. verum, (with ego); ; ; with verumtamen,; with tamen,; ; with sed tamen,; ; ; ; ; with ceterum,.—
Sometimes with pregn. reference to the speaker, for my part, as far as I am concerned: equidem me Caesaris militem dici volui; vos me, etc.,: equidem doleo non me tuis litteris certiorem fieri,: quod equidem sciam,; cf. .—Cf. Hand Turs. II. pp. 422-437.

ĕquus, i (
gen. plur. equūm, ; ), m.
Sanscr. acvas; Gr. ἵππος (ἴκκος); cf. Epŏna; root, ak-, to be sharp or swift; cf. Gr. ἄκρος, ὠκύς; Lat. acus, ocior
, a horse, steed, charger.
Prop.
In gen. (cf.: caballus, canterius, mannus),; ; ; ; Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 441 ed. Vahlen); ; ; ; et saep.: equus = equa,.—Offered as a sacrifice to Mars, Paul. ex , and p. 178, 24 sq. Müll.; cf. ; and v. October: EQVO PVBLICO ORNATVS, EXORNATVS, HONORATVS, etc.; or, ellipt., EQVO PVBLICO, very often

in inscriptions; v. ; ; ; 1952; 2456; 2865 al.—In another sense: equi publici,post-horses,.—Equo vehi, advehi, ire, desilire, equum conscendere, flectere, in equum ascendere, equo citato, concitato, etc., see under these verbs.—

In partic.
Of cavalry, in the phrase, equis virisque (viri = pedites; cf. eques and vir), adverb., with horse and foot, i. e. with might and main, with tooth and nail, ; ; also: equis, viris,; ; cf. ; and in the order, viris equisque,.—
Transf., of race-horses: ego cursu corrigam tarditatem tum equis, tum vero, quoniam scribis poëma ab eo nostrum probari, quadrigis poeticis,i. e. in prose and poetry,, a (see the passage in connection).—
Transf.
In plur. (like ἵπποι in Homer), a chariot, .—
The wind, ; .—
In mal. part., ; ; ; .—
Prov.: equi donati dentes non inspiciuntur, we don't look a gift horse in the mouth, ad Ephes. prooem.—
Meton.
Equus bipes, a sea-horse, ; Auct. Pervig. Ven. 10: fluviatilis,a river-horse, hippopotamus,.—
Equus ligneus, like the Homeric ἁλὸς ἵππος, a ship, .—
The Trojan horse, ; ; ; ; — *
Trop., of a secret conspiracy, .—
A battering-ram, because shaped like a horse; afterwards called aries,.—
The constellation Pegasus, ; ; ; .—
